extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially speculative-fiction authors) focused on worldbuilding
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on choosing between drilling deeply into a few world elements versus covering many elements shallowly, and how to execute deep worldbuilding so it serves story and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth vs. Width decision
rubrics_metrics.description: How do you decide between digging one really deep, narrow well, and digging one really wide, shallow ocean?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the tradeoff: wide/shallow worldbuilding can create the impression of scale but feel repetitive or thin (the 'ocean an inch deep' / 4000 copy-pasted dungeons example). Deep worldbuilding makes fewer elements feel richly realized. You must choose which approach to take based on story needs and your available time; you can't do both everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth comes from causal chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth comes from causal chains, how things are linked together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For deep detail, show why something arose, the need that caused it, and how it ripples through the rest of the world. Map links between origin → use → societal consequences rather than treating an item as an isolated detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show history and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A deep element has history and demonstrable consequences in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't just name an artifact/technology/magic—show its history and consequences. Ask: why did this appear, who benefits or suffers, and what societal changes follow? Avoid focusing only on personal tolls; think broadly about social impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how tech/magic works when it solves plot problems
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character uses something—science, technology, magic—to solve a problem, you need to know how it works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never handwave important plot mechanics with 'then she did some science.' Do enough study to write convincingly; Dan used virology study to write a convincing cure plot. This prevents plot holes and sells the scene to knowledgeable readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drill deep on a few branches, not everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a handful of technological/magical/social branches and drill intensely into them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick three or four branches to explore in depth and trace their ramifications across society, infrastructure, and daily life (example: self-driving cars — parking behavior affects city layout and traffic). This yields interesting, integrated story ideas without requiring exhaustive depth everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can't go deep on everything; prioritize
rubrics_metrics.description: You must prioritize which elements to deepen because you lack resources to do all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus depth where it most serves the story; treat other areas with a light touch or go wide. Use shallow coverage to plant seeds for later deep dives. Don't try to make everything equally interesting—that often yields uniformly bland worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the element that produces 'surprising yet inevitable' outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth should produce moments that feel surprising but also inevitable given the world's logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate the one element (or combination) whose causal network gives you the pieces needed for the story to unfold in the desired way. Make that the locus of your deep research so plot developments feel earned rather than contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use light touches as seeds for later stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Touch lightly on many topics to 'pitch' ideas you can catch in later books or scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A light mention can plant an idea for future exploration; it's a deliberate shallow choice, not sloppiness. This lets you hint at breadth while reserving depth for elements you later choose to expand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audition characters to avoid stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Create multiple plausible variants of a character from the same background and choose one to appear on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft three or four different faces/backgrounds/attitudes for a side-character role; select the one who best serves the scene and keep the others 'real' in your head. This practice helps avoid one-dimensional stereotypes and makes the chosen character feel embedded in a lived world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate similar-background characters by primary driver (axes of power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make characters from the same culture express different priorities by assigning different primary drivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the axes of power—role, relationship, hierarchy, ability—to define each character's chief motivation. For example, two astronauts with the same background can be distinct if one is driven by duty/relationship and the other by status/hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization is action
rubrics_metrics.description: Who a character is has very little to do with where they come from and everything to do with what they choose and what they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show character through choices and behavior (e.g., the four hobbits are distinguished by actions). Especially for secondary characters you can't enter into their heads, rely on actions to reveal personality rather than background exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus depth on plot‑critical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which element(s) the plot hinges on and concentrate deep research there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a plot turn depends on a scientific/magical/technological detail (e.g., a cure, or political/climate conditions), prioritize understanding that element thoroughly so the plot mechanics are believable and internally consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to discard or omit research that doesn’t serve the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Do research freely but omit interesting facts that won't move the story forward or will distract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research can generate fascinating asides (Howard's Saturn rings anecdote) that nevertheless don't belong in the book. Inclusion should be governed by whether the detail advances character, theme, or plot; otherwise leave it out.
